varm

varm is a fast R package for frequentist and Bayesian vector autoregressions (VAR, BVAR, TVP-VAR with stochastic volatility), structural identification and local projections (LP). The estimators, bootstraps, MCMC samplers and identification loops run in compiled Rcpp/RcppArmadillo code. A 3-variable hierarchical BVAR draws 1000 posterior samples in about 0.1 s, a full 3-variable local projection takes about 0.4 ms, and results are checked against vars, BVAR, lpirfs, lm + sandwich and exact posteriors to between 10−1310^{-13} and Monte Carlo accuracy (see Validation and the validation report).

The design idea is one currency for uncertainty: the bootstrap, the asymptotic Monte Carlo and each Bayesian sampler return a varm_draws object of reduced-form draws (B,Σ)(B, \Sigma). irf(), fevd(), hd() and forecast(), and every identification scheme (id_chol(), id_longrun(), id_sign(), id_given(), …) work on that object, so a new estimator inherits all identification schemes and a new identification scheme works with every estimator.

The package is experimental (version 0.1.0); see Limitations.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("kvasilopoulos/varm")

A C++ toolchain is required (the package compiles RcppArmadillo code). The reference implementations used in the tests (vars, BVAR, lpirfs, bsvars, sandwich, mvtnorm) are in Suggests.

Tidy by design

  • Tibbles with broom column names. tidy(), glance() and augment() (re-exported from generics) return tibbles with term, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, horizon, level. as_tibble() is an alias of tidy() for IRF, FEVD, forecast, historical decomposition, LP and Bayesian objects.
  • tidyselect arguments. Every argument that names variables takes bare names, strings, positions or helpers: lp(yraw, shock = rate, contemp = c(infl, unemp)), id_chol(order = c(infl, unemp, rate)), autoplot(ir, shocks = rate), varm(df, p = 2, vars = c(infl, rate)).
  • ggplot2 for every result. autoplot() returns a ggplot for VAR/BVAR IRF, FEVD, forecast and historical decomposition objects, draws, MCMC diagnostics, TVP-VAR paths and every local-projection result; plot() prints the same object. The figure is yours to modify with +.
  • One theme and palette. theme_varm() and the colour-blind-safe varm_palette() are used by all plots and available for your own.
  • Pipe-friendly. The data or model is always the first argument and there is no hidden state: yraw |> varm(p = 2) |> irf(horizon = 16) |> autoplot().

Thirty seconds with each family

All examples use yraw, three quarterly US series (inflation infl, unemployment unemp, interest rate rate; Koop and Korobilis, 1953Q1-2006Q3). Each ends in an autoplot() figure and shows one tidy() and one glance() call.

VAR: impulse responses with bootstrap bands 

library(varm)
fit <- varm(yraw, p = 2)
fit
#> <varm> VAR(2) with 3 variables, 213 effective observations
#> logLik = -338.416; max |eigenvalue| = 0.946
#> 
#>             infl   unemp    rate
#> infl.l1   1.5378 -0.0095  0.5457
#> unemp.l1 -0.2809  1.3297 -0.6475
#> rate.l1  -0.0571 -0.0210  0.7766

#> rate.l2   0.0580  0.0457  0.1232
#> const     0.2872  0.3654  0.0052
tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 21 × 8
#>    response term     estimate std.error statistic  p.value  conf.low conf.high

Responses to a policy-rate shock (recursive identification, rate ordered last), with 68% and 90% wild-bootstrap bands. autoplot(ir) without shocks gives the full shock-by-response grid:

set.seed(1)
ir <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 16, ci = "wild", nboot = 1000)
tidy(ir)
#> # A tibble: 306 × 7
#>    response shock horizon estimate level conf.low  conf.high
#>    <fct>    <fct>   <int>    <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>
#>  1 infl     infl        0   0.308    0.9   0.297   0.311    
#>  2 unemp    infl        0  -0.0117   0.9  -0.0204  0.0000663
#>  3 rate     infl        0   0.0877   0.9   0.0505  0.104    
#>  4 infl     unemp       0   0        0.9   0       0        
#>  5 unemp    unemp       0   0.332    0.9   0.321   0.334    
#>  6 rate     unemp       0  -0.268    0.9  -0.285  -0.235    
#>  7 infl     rate        0   0        0.9   0       0        
#>  8 unemp    rate        0   0        0.9   0       0        
#>  9 rate     rate        0   0.715    0.9   0.681   0.719    
#> 10 infl     infl        1   0.472    0.9   0.410   0.497    
#> # ℹ 296 more rows
autoplot(ir, shocks = rate)

BVAR with stochastic volatility

A triangular (equation-by-equation) Gibbs sampler with a Minnesota prior and stochastic volatility:

set.seed(1)
bfit <- bvarm(yraw, p = 2, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), sv = TRUE,
              ndraw = 2000, nburn = 1000)
bfit
#> <bvarm> triangular-minnesota-sv BVAR(2), K = 3, 2000 posterior draws
#> 
#> posterior mean of B:
#>             infl   unemp    rate
#> infl.l1   1.2908 -0.0149  0.1870
#> unemp.l1 -0.1210  1.2135 -0.3127
#> rate.l1  -0.0022 -0.0097  1.0203
#> infl.l2  -0.2992  0.0483 -0.1303
#> unemp.l2  0.0739 -0.2804  0.2884
#> rate.l2  -0.0033  0.0231 -0.0959
#> const     0.3075  0.1943  0.3286
tidy(bfit)
#> # A tibble: 21 × 6
#>    response term     estimate std.error conf.low conf.high
#>    <chr>    <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 infl     infl.l1   1.29       0.0548   1.20      1.38  
#>  2 infl     unemp.l1 -0.121      0.0346  -0.177    -0.0632
#>  3 infl     rate.l1  -0.00223    0.0168  -0.0299    0.0263
#>  4 infl     infl.l2  -0.299      0.0563  -0.391    -0.207 
#>  5 infl     unemp.l2  0.0739     0.0329   0.0195    0.127 
#>  6 infl     rate.l2  -0.00335    0.0151  -0.0297    0.0203

#>  8 unemp    infl.l1  -0.0149     0.0417  -0.0843    0.0530
#>  9 unemp    unemp.l1  1.21       0.0544   1.12      1.30  
#> 10 unemp    rate.l1  -0.00968    0.0173  -0.0370    0.0193
#> # ℹ 11 more rows
glance(bfit)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>       K     p  nobs ndraw method                  logml accept
#>   <int> <int> <int> <int> <chr>                   <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1     3     2   213  2000 triangular-minnesota-sv    NA     NA

autoplot(bfit, type = "coef") plots the coefficient posteriors, and volatility() returns the posterior-mean shock volatilities, which are one tidy()-style reshape away from a ggplot:

library(ggplot2)
vol <- volatility(bfit)
d <- data.frame(
  quarter = rep(seq(1953.25 + 2 * 0.25, by = 0.25, length.out = nrow(vol)), ncol(vol)),
  variable = rep(colnames(vol), each = nrow(vol)),
  volatility = as.vector(vol)
)
ggplot(d, aes(quarter, volatility, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = varm_palette(3)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Posterior mean shock volatility", colour = NULL) +
  theme_varm()

The default prior of bvarm() is instead the conjugate hierarchical Minnesota prior of Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri (2015), with exact draws for the coefficients and a Metropolis step for the hyperparameters. Both return a bvarm object, and irf(bfit, id = id_chol()) works the same way as for fit.

Local projections

shock and contemp are tidyselect arguments (bare names, strings or c()); contemp lists the variables ordered before the shock, which reproduces the recursive identification used above.

lpf <- lp(yraw, shock = rate, contemp = c(infl, unemp), horizon = 16, lags = 2,
          lag_augment = TRUE)
lpf
#> <lpm> local projection of infl, unemp, rate on 'rate', horizons 0..16 (3 lags, HC)
#>       infl   unemp    rate
#> 0   0.0000  0.0000  1.0000
#> 1  -0.0590 -0.0243  0.7763
#> 4  -0.0117  0.0456  0.6506
#> 8  -0.1030  0.2381  0.2098
#> 12 -0.5391  0.1760 -0.1398
#> 16 -0.6921  0.0634 -0.4354
tidy(lpf)
#> # A tibble: 102 × 7
#>    horizon response  estimate std.error level  conf.low conf.high

For the same shock the LP and VAR responses are close but not identical; compare_lp_var() quantifies it.

Features

Status column: validated = agrees with a named reference implementation or an exact result in the tests or validation/; tested = unit tests of correctness (against a hand computation, a simulation with known truth, or an invariant) but no external reference; new = recently added, documented, consistency-tested only. Details in the validation report.

Method Function Reference Status

Benchmarks

Seconds of elapsed time per 1000 retained posterior draws, simulated VAR(4) with T=250T = 250, Apple M4 Pro, R 4.6.1, OpenBLAS, single-threaded (OMP_NUM_THREADS=1), nothing else running, installed package. Reproduce with Rscript validation/bayes.R s8.

sampler K = 3 K = 7 K = 20
bvarm() conjugate, fixed hyperparameters 0.003 0.010 0.061
bvarm() conjugate, hierarchical (optimiser + 500 burn-in) 0.054 0.177 1.271
bvarm() triangular, Minnesota, homoskedastic 0.019 0.110 1.312
bvarm() triangular, Minnesota + stochastic volatility 0.112 0.382 2.979
BVAR::bvar() (hierarchical λ\lambda) 0.157 0.259 0.899
bsvars::bsvar_sv() (structural SV) 1.35 4.64 not run

Other timings on yraw (T=215T = 215, K=3K = 3, p=2p = 2):

task time
tvpvar(), SV + time-varying AtA_t + full QQ, 10000 draws + 2000 burn-in about 8 s
lp() for one shock, 3 responses, horizons 0-16 about 0.5 ms
varm() OLS fit about 0.05 ms
1000 wild-bootstrap draws of the VAR(2) 0.02 s
irf() with 1000 wild-bootstrap draws, horizon 16 0.03 s
bvarm() hierarchical, 10000 draws + 2000 burn-in 0.39 s
bvarm() triangular + SV, 10000 draws + 2000 burn-in 2.4 s

Reading the table honestly: the conjugate samplers are very fast and the hierarchical one beats BVAR::bvar() for K=3K = 3 (about 2x), is level at K=7K = 7, and is slower at K=20K = 20 (3.6 s against 1.6 s). The triangular samplers are a different model class (no BVAR counterpart); their cost rises from 0.05 s (K=3K = 3) to 5.7 s (K=20K = 20) in the homoskedastic case. tvpvar() is a long-running sampler: about 3 ms per sweep at p=2p = 2, and the cost increases steeply with the lag length. Timings depend on the machine, the BLAS and the settings, and were measured in single runs.

Validation

Checks run live in the validation report; the longer ones are in validation/. The unit-test suite (tests/testthat) has 846 expectations and runs in about 17 s.

Module Reference Agreement (max abs. difference unless stated)
VAR coefficients, covariance, log-likelihood, IC vars ≤\le 6e-13
Cholesky IRF, FEVD, point forecast vars 4e-13 (IRF), 3e-13 (FEVD), 5e-12 (forecast)
Blanchard-Quah impact matrix vars::BQ 1e-13
LP coefficient, Newey-West and HC1 s.e. lm + sandwich 3e-13
State-dependent LP (IRF and HAC band half-widths) lpirfs::lp_nl 7.5e-13
Hierarchical BVAR log posterior at matched ψ\psi BVAR::bvar 7e-13 (relative 2e-15)
Hierarchical hyperparameter posterior means exact quadrature, BVAR MCMC within 3% (Monte Carlo error)
Triangular sampler, homoskedastic exact semi-conjugate posterior max abs. zz 2.2
Stochastic-volatility update Geweke joint-distribution test all absolute zz below 1.1
Haar rotations, sign-restriction acceptance rates exact laws (KS, 1/21/2, 1/41/4) KS statistic 0.003 or less
TVP-VAR, constant limit OLS 4e-3 (Monte Carlo error)
OLS VAR, NW posterior, Cholesky IRF, FEVD, HD, sign and zero restrictions BEAR toolbox (MATLAB), via R ports checked against BEAR’s stored .mat results 1e-12 or better; sampled quantities within Monte Carlo error
Minnesota NW marginal likelihood and posterior, with and without dummy priors BEAR toolbox no dummies 1e-9; sum-of-coefficients 1e-9; combined dummies 0.05 log units (open)
Cholesky and long-run IRF, FEVD, HD, LP, IV-LP VAR-Toolbox (MATLAB), via R ports 1e-5 or better (3e-14 for long-run)
Minnesota marginal likelihood, IRF, forecasts, proxy-SVAR, LP BVAR_ (MATLAB), via R ports 1e-7 or better once conventions are matched

The three MATLAB toolboxes (BEAR, VAR-Toolbox, BVAR_) were compared by porting their .m algorithms to R, not by running MATLAB. The dated diary in validation/DIARY.md lists every test, the convention differences (degrees of freedom, lag-decay exponent, bootstrap rescaling, proxy centring) and what is not covered.

Limitations

Found by the validation scripts, in order of how likely they are to matter:

  • Draw-based IRF bands under-cover in short, persistent or heteroskedastic samples. For a VAR(1) with ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9 and T=200T = 200, 90% bands cover 81% (iid bootstrap), 75% (wild), 88% (Monte Carlo) and 89% (bias-corrected iid bootstrap); with heteroskedastic errors every method covers only 61-75%.
  • The proxy-SVAR wild bootstrap does not cover the impact response (13-21% coverage of nominal 90% in validation/proxy-coverage.R). Use type = "mbb" (default of proxy_draws()) or varm_proxy_robust().
  • Sup-t bands from lp_supt() under-cover: 78% whole-path coverage with HAC errors (84% with lag-augmented HC errors) at nominal 90%.
  • Stochastic-volatility calibration is slightly low: 83% coverage of the volatility-of-volatility parameter and 88% of the volatility path at nominal 90% (simulation-based calibration, 60 replications).
  • TVP-VAR results depend on the prior (tvp_prior(kQ = )); coverage of simulated coefficient paths ranged from 56% to 79% across two settings.
  • The hierarchical sampler mixes slowly: effective sample sizes of 70-160 for the hyperparameters in 3000 draws of one chain. Use mcmc_diagnostics().
  • id_zerosign() is unweighted: the ARRW importance weights are not implemented, so bands under partial zero restrictions are approximate.
  • No missing values, no VECM or cointegration, no panel or global VAR, no mixed-frequency models, no frequentist penalised (lasso) VAR, no narrative restrictions. See the literature map for packages that cover these.
  • varm_proxy_arw() and varm_proxy_gkr() are new and have no external replication; in a 50-replication simulation the 90% ARW band covered 91% and the conventional single-prior GKR band only 65% for a set-identified shock (the robust region 91%).
  • Speed: BVAR::bvar() is faster at K=20K = 20 for the hierarchical prior.

Literature map

The full discussion is in vignette("choosing-a-method"). Entries are from the awesome-var list.

Area Packages Relation to varm
Core VAR vars, svars, tsDyn overlap on estimation and recursive/long-run/sign IRFs (varm agrees with vars to rounding error); no diagnostic tests, VECM or threshold models
Hierarchical BVAR BVAR, bvartools same GLP prior (log posterior agrees with BVAR at matched ψ\psi); varm adds triangular, SV, SSVS and horseshoe samplers
Bayesian SVAR bsvars, bsvarSIGNs, bpvars complementary: use them for narrative restrictions, weighted zero+sign inference and identification through heteroskedasticity
Time variation bvarsv, bvhar, mfbvar varm has tvpvar() and bvarm(sv = TRUE); no mixed frequency
High-dimensional BigVAR, bigtime, VARshrink varm covers Bayesian shrinkage only
Panel and global VAR panelvar, pvars, BGVAR varm has panel LP (lp_panel()) but no panel VAR
Local projections lpirfs, sovereign varm matches lpirfs::lp_nl; adds smooth LP, sup-t bands, LP-IV, lag augmentation
External instruments varexternal, Plagborg-Moller code varm_proxy*() family and lp(iv = )

Also in the awesome-var list and not covered by varm: the MATLAB toolboxes (VAR Toolbox, BEAR, IRIS, BVAR_), Python (statsmodels, sktime), Julia (VectorAutoregressions.jl, LocalProjections.jl) and EViews/Stata implementations.

  8. Choosing a method - vignette("choosing-a-method")
  9. Validation report - vignette("validation")

The reference index lists every function with its tidy and plot methods (tidy.varm_irf, autoplot.varm_irf, theme_varm, …).

The method-by-method index with definitions and references is docs-src/methods-index.md; the change log is in NEWS.md.

Citation

There is no paper yet. Until there is, cite the package:

citation("varm")

and the original references of the method you use (see the Features table).

Contributing

Bug reports and pull requests are welcome at https://github.com/kvasilopoulos/varm/issues. Please include a minimal reproducible example. Changes to an estimator should come with a test that compares against an independent implementation or an exact result, and a note in validation/ for anything stochastic. To run the checks from the package root:

Rscript validation/run-all.R      # unit tests
Rscript validation/bayes.R        # heavier statistical validation
